questions.q: At the start of a match, an FTC robot must fit inside...
wrong: A 24-by-24-by-24-inch cube
A 12-by-12-by-12-inch cube
A 36-by-36-by-36-inch cube
questions.explain: FTC robots must start each match fitting inside an 18 × 18 × 18 inch cube. They can expand once the match begins, but they start compact.

questions.correct: The robot's brain — it runs Android and your Java code
wrong: A spare battery pack that powers the drive motors
The controller the human driver holds in a match
A sensor that only measures the robot's ground speed
questions.explain: The Control Hub is the robot's brain. It runs Android, executes your Java, and has motor ports, servo ports, and a built-in IMU.

questions.q: How do you add more motor and servo ports?
questions.correct: Connect an Expansion Hub to the Control Hub
wrong: Solder some extra wires onto the main battery
Install a second copy of the Android app
Swap the gamepad for a much bigger controller
questions.explain: The Expansion Hub plugs into the Control Hub and adds 4 more motor ports, 6 more servo ports, and extra sensor ports when one hub isn't enough.

wrong: Four small AA alkaline batteries
A cord plugged into a wall outlet
A solar panel on the robot's top
questions.explain: Everything on the robot runs off a single 12-volt rechargeable battery. The power switch has to be quick to reach in case you need to cut power.

questions.correct: The touchscreen drivers use to pick and start programs
wrong: The brain that runs your Java code on the robot
The wheel base that carries the robot around
A sensor that tracks the robot's heading angle
questions.explain: The Driver Hub is the touchscreen device drivers use to select programs, start the match, and read telemetry. Controllers plug into it over USB.

questions.q: How many controllers can plug into the Driver Hub?
wrong: Only one, which is called gamepad1
Four, one for each alliance member
None; it uses only its own touchscreen
questions.explain: Two controllers plug in: gamepad1 and gamepad2. Usually driver 1 handles movement and driver 2 handles the mechanisms.

questions.q: What are the two phases of an FTC match?
wrong: Practice (1 minute) then the Finals (5 minutes)
Setup (2 minutes) then Cleanup (30 seconds)
Offense (2 minutes) then Defense (2 minutes)
questions.explain: A match is a 30-second Autonomous phase (no human input) followed by a roughly 2-minute Tele-Op phase where drivers control the robot.

questions.q: During Autonomous, who controls the robot?
questions.correct: No one — the robot runs your code by itself
wrong: The driver, using only the left stick
A referee, using a special handheld remote
The judges, from the main scoring table
questions.explain: Autonomous means no human input for the first 30 seconds — the robot follows the plan your code lays out entirely on its own.

questions.q: When you press a button, what path does the signal take?
questions.correct: Controller to Driver Hub to Control Hub to your code
wrong: Controller straight to the motor, skipping the hubs
Control Hub to Driver Hub to the controller only
Driver Hub to the battery and then back again
questions.explain: A press travels controller → Driver Hub → Control Hub → your Java code → the motor, many times a second. Your code sits in the middle deciding what happens.

questions.q: Who decides what each button and stick actually does?
questions.correct: The programmer, through the code they write
wrong: The controller's factory settings, permanently
The head referee, before each match starts
The battery, based on its current charge level
questions.explain: The same hardware can behave completely differently depending on the code. As the programmer, YOU decide what every button and joystick does.

questions.q: What are most FTC robots built from?
questions.correct: Pre-made kit parts like goBILDA and REV, no welding
wrong: Custom welded steel made in a real machine shop
Wood and glue cut apart with a hand saw
Only 3D-printed plastic, with no metal at all
questions.explain: Most teams build from pre-fabricated kits (goBILDA, REV, Actobotics, Tetrix). No welding or machining is required — parts bolt together like heavy-duty building sets.

questions.q: What sensor is built into the Control Hub?
questions.correct: An IMU that can track the robot's heading
wrong: A camera that records the entire match
A GPS that reads the robot's map location
A microphone that listens for the whistle
questions.explain: The Control Hub has a built-in IMU (inertial measurement unit) that can track rotation and heading — you'll use it in a later lesson.

questions.q: Typically, how do two drivers split the work?
questions.correct: One drives the base, the other runs mechanisms
wrong: Both drive the base at the exact same time
One plays offense, the other watches the clock
They take turns, one minute on and one off
questions.explain: Usually gamepad1's driver handles movement and gamepad2's driver runs the mechanisms (intake, shooter, etc.). Splitting roles keeps a hectic match manageable.

questions.q: How big is the FTC playing field?
wrong: About 6 by 6 feet
About 20 by 20 feet
About 3 by 3 feet
questions.explain: The FTC field is roughly 12 × 12 feet, walled in on all sides, and shared by both alliances during a match.

questions.q: Can the same robot hardware behave differently with new code?
questions.correct: Yes — the code decides how the hardware acts
wrong: No — hardware always behaves one single fixed way
Only if you also rewire all of the motors
Only during the autonomous part of a match
questions.explain: Absolutely. The hardware is fixed, but the code decides what it does — the same motors and buttons can drive, shoot, or lift depending on what you program.
